1913 · 1916
Walter Hines Page bought a thousand acres of pine, and named it Garran Hill.
From London, 1917
Ambassador to the Court of St James's. From the embassy, he wrote home about the farm. The farm. The farm.
Built 1915 – 1916
By the Pinehurst Company. The same men then building Pinehurst.
Hollycrest · 1959 – 1984
Betty Dumaine came, and stayed twenty-five years.
1916 · Today
The same gate has stood open for one hundred and ten years.
The man who longed for it
He built it to come home to. He never came home to it.

Publisher, Doubleday founder, and United States Ambassador to Great Britain through the years the world came apart. He had his son Ralph build the farm and wrote home for it constantly. He resigned the embassy and sailed back gravely ill in 1918, reached Pinehurst, and died that December. He remains the only American diplomat of the First World War honored with a tablet at Westminster Abbey.

The House
The Threshold
Four columns. Full entablature. The fanlight is original to 1916.

Through the door, a two-story entry. The oak handrail runs unbroken from volute to landing. You see the whole depth of the house before you take three steps. The proportions are correct because the drawings survived.

Move through the house the way it was built to be walked. Room by room, in order.

The Grounds
A saltwater pool inside a brick-walled garden. Two lighted courts. The Wee Cottage.
At the back of the grounds
She would leave flowers at his grave. Someone still does.

Betty Dumaine loved one horse above the rest, an Irish hunter named Blue Fox. When he died she buried him at the back of the grounds, under slate, and marked it in brass. The marker is still there.
